s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Architects treat the axis as the most basic organizing device for forms and spaces. To function as a true linear axis capable of structuring a composition, what must such a line possess?
o: By acting as a continuous line, plane, or volume that links, gathers, and anchors disparate elements through its structural and visual continuity.
It is an imaginary, straight line that possesses qualities of length and direction, demanding terminating elements at both ends to anchor its visual force.
By utilizing the laws of physics, balancing elements of smaller visual mass at great distances from a virtual center against elements of larger visual mass closer to the center.
By acting as a continuous line, plane, or volume that links, gathers, and anchors disparate elements through its structural and visual continuity.
n: Answer: B — Ching: an axis is an imaginary line of length and direction that requires terminating elements at both ends to anchor its visual force. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q1)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: A datum is often called a powerful ordering device. By what mechanism does a datum bring coherence to an otherwise scattered, mixed group of forms and spaces?
o: By acting as a continuous line, plane, or volume that links, gathers, and anchors disparate elements through its structural and visual continuity.
It is an imaginary, straight line that possesses qualities of length and direction, demanding terminating elements at both ends to anchor its visual force.
By acting as a continuous line, plane, or volume that links, gathers, and anchors disparate elements through its structural and visual continuity.
By utilizing the laws of physics, balancing elements of smaller visual mass at great distances from a virtual center against elements of larger visual mass closer to the center.
n: Answer: A — Ching: a datum is a continuous line, plane, or volume whose regularity gathers and organizes a scattered set of forms. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q2)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Hierarchy as an ordering principle lets one element read as dominant within a composition through three basic strategies. Which option below is NOT one of those strategies?
o: Giving the element a distinct shape that contrasts with the rest.
Making the element noticeably larger or bulkier than its neighbors.
Positioning the element at a strategic node or termination point.
Hiding the element entirely so it cannot be seen from outside.
n: Answer: D — Ching's three ways an element achieves hierarchical dominance are by size, shape, and strategic placement — concealment is the opposite of dominance. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q3)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Repetition on its own is generic. What has to happen for that repetition to read instead as genuine architectural rhythm?
o: Every repeating module must switch to a new material each time it recurs.
The repeated units must be laid out along a curving, undulating plane.
The repeated units must fall into an organized sequence or alternating pattern that guides the eye through the composition.
Exactly three structural components must repeat, no more and no fewer.
n: Answer: C — Simple repetition becomes rhythm only when the repeated elements form a structured or alternating sequence that guides the eye. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q4)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In the morphology of architectural design, what does the operation called 'Transformation' set out to accomplish?
o: Making a building's exterior appearance give no clue whatsoever about its interior layout.
Reshaping a base form step by step until none of its original structure can be recognized.
Progressively stripping a primitive volume of its core structure or identity.
Reworking a base form through a sequence of geometric moves while its underlying grid and identity remain recognizable.
n: Answer: B — Transformation is the incremental alteration of a form while its underlying grid/identity remains recognizable, per Ching's design vocabulary. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q5)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Under what circumstance can a composition that is asymmetrical in layout still read as balanced and orderly?
o: When lighter visual masses sit near the central axis and heavier masses are pushed farther away from it.
When a heavy element positioned near the center is counterweighted by a lighter element set well out toward the edge.
Asymmetrical compositions are inherently incapable of achieving true design balance.
When a large mass is kept close to the center and every lighter element nearby is simply removed.
n: Answer: B — Asymmetrical balance works like a lever: a small mass far from the center can balance a large mass near it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q6)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: An architect adding a modern wing to a classical masonry library must respect the existing structure. How does the principle of transformation guide that intervention?
o: By studying the old building's grid, rhythms, and proportions and then applying those same rules literally to a new design.
It insists the new wing be an exact, unaltered copy of the historic building.
By refining the historic building's structural bays, rhythms, and proportions, then reinterpreting that classical library for a new use.
By tearing down the historic structure and rebuilding the whole thing in mirrored glass.
n: Answer: A — In adaptive reuse, architects study the historic grid, rhythm, and proportion of the old structure and extend those same rules into the new design. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q7)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Radial symmetry, as a spatial organizing device, is best illustrated by which of these layouts?
o: A narrow hospital wing lined with matching patient rooms along both sides.
A circular altar ringed by identical stone piers and seating segments radiating outward.
A tower that twists a full 90 degrees as it climbs skyward.
A loose scatter of timber huts strung along a winding mountain river.
n: Answer: A — Radial symmetry is a central element with identical parts repeating outward around it, as in a circular altar with radiating piers. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q8)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Proportion refers to the measurable relationship between a part's dimensions and those of the whole. How, fundamentally, does 'scale' differ from 'proportion'?
o: Proportion concerns how a building's size compares to a human being, while scale concerns the part-to-whole ratio.
Proportion describes how a part relates to the other parts, while scale describes how the object's size reads against some external reference.
Proportion must be worked out in metric units, while scale can only be computed in imperial units.
Scale is set by the structural engineer, while proportion is a decision left to the client.
n: Answer: C — Proportion is the relationship of parts to each other and the whole; scale compares an object's size to an external reference, usually the human body. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q9)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In the Classical Orders, all column heights, entablatures, and spacing intervals derive from a single base unit. What serves as that module?
o: The base diameter of the column shaft
The standardized length of a Royal Egyptian cubit rod.
The total height of the client's entrance portal.
A random dimension chosen by the head mason on the morning of construction.
n: Answer: C — In the Classical Orders, the module is the base diameter of the column shaft, from which all other dimensions are derived. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q10)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Palladio and other Renaissance architects built proportioning systems on musical consonances. What belief underpinned that choice?
o: A belief that buildings needed hollow, resonant walls to amplify indoor orchestras.
A conviction that the same ratios governing music and science reflected a cosmic order fit to be applied to building dimensions.
Using musical ratios simply to bewilder rival builders with no musical training.
Applying musical harmony's mathematical ratios to a structure's dimensions as an expression of divine order.
n: Answer: C — Renaissance theorists like Palladio believed musical harmonic ratios reflected a divine, cosmic order and translated those ratios directly into building proportions. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q11)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: 'Anthropometry,' used as a proportioning system in spatial design, centers on measuring what, primarily?
o: The study of how historical monuments weather over centuries.
The mathematical calculation of structural wind shear on skyscraper facades.
The measurement of the physical dimensions, operational reach, and clearance requirements of the human body.
The tracking of microclimatic humidity shifts inside standard concrete rooms.
n: Answer: B — Anthropometry is the study of human body dimensions, reach, and clearance requirements used to size architectural elements. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q12)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: The Fibonacci sequence (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21…) ties closely to which system of architectural proportion?
o: The Golden Section
The Anthropometric Clearance Matrix
The Classical Tuscan Order
The Inaka-ma Fixed Column Grid
n: Answer: B — The Fibonacci sequence approximates the Golden Ratio, the basis of the Golden Section proportioning system. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q13)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Le Corbusier devised a universal proportioning system that combined the Golden Ratio with human bodily measurements. What is it called?
o: The Anthropometric Matrix
The Modulor
The Golden Section
The Ken
n: Answer: B — Le Corbusier's Modulor combined the Golden Ratio with human body proportions into a universal scale. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q14)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Among the Vitruvian triad, which term stands for utility — a building's spatial function and the efficient layout of its program?
o: Firmitas
Utilitas
Venustas
Commoditas
n: Answer: C — In the Vitruvian triad, Utilitas refers to function/utility, Firmitas to structure, and Venustas to beauty. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q15)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which spatial relationship describes a smaller space fully surrounded, on all sides, by a larger three-dimensional space?
o: Interlocking spaces
Spaces linked by a common space
Adjacent spaces
Space within a space
n: Answer: A — 'Space within a space' occurs when a larger volume fully contains and encloses a smaller one. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q16)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which layout type places one dominant central space at the hub, with several linear arms radiating outward like spokes?
o: Cluster organization
Centralized organization
Radial organization
Grid organization
n: Answer: B — Radial organization extends linear arms outward from a dominant central space, like spokes on a wheel. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q17)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: A repeating three-dimensional matrix of structural bays that governs placement, form, and program boundaries describes which spatial system?
o: Linear organization
Centralized organization
Clustered organization
Grid organization
n: Answer: C — Grid organization uses a repeating three-dimensional matrix of bays to regulate form and layout. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q18)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Edward T. Hall coined a term for the study of the psychological and cultural distances people keep from one another in social settings. What is that term?
o: Kinesics
Proxemics
Anthropometrics
Ergonomics
n: Answer: C — Edward T. Hall coined 'proxemics' for the study of culturally determined personal spatial distances. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q19)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Proxemics defines a zone of personal space running roughly 1.5 to 4 feet, typically reserved for close friends and family. What is this zone called?
o: Social Distance
Personal Distance
Public Distance
Intimate Distance
n: Answer: B — Hall's Personal Distance zone (about 1.5–4 ft) is reserved for close friends and family. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q20)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: A traditional Japanese proportioning module governs both timber column spacing and standard floor-mat sizing. What is it called?
o: Shaku
Tokonoma
Tatami
Ken
n: Answer: B — The Ken is a Japanese modular unit that governs both the structural column grid and standard tatami mat sizes. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q21)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In structural terms, what is the name for a beam or slab that projects horizontally beyond its supporting column, held up over open space by internal tension and counterweighting?
o: Portal Frame
Truss
Tie-Rod
Cantilever
n: Answer: B — A cantilever is a horizontal member that projects beyond its support, held by internal tension/counterbalance rather than an end support. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q22)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: When every visual and physical element of a composition works together so no single part pulls attention from the whole concept, which design principle has been achieved?
o: Contrast
Emphasis
Contrast and Variety
Unity
n: Answer: C — Unity is achieved when all compositional elements are harmonized around one overarching concept, with nothing distracting from it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q23)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In composition, what name is given to the kind of rhythm produced when an element's size, color, or shape shifts gradually and continuously across a sequence of spaces — a step-by-step, predictable visual progression?
o: Monotonous rhythm
Progressive rhythm
Static rhythm
Alternating rhythm
n: Answer: B — Progressive rhythm is created by a step-by-step, predictable change in an element's size, shape, or spacing. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q24)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which type of scale describes a design so massive it makes people feel small, deliberately projecting the power of an institution, state, or religion?
o: Human Scale
Anthropometric Scale
Monumental Scale
Intimate Scale
n: Answer: C — Monumental scale intentionally overwhelms the individual to project institutional, state, or religious power. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q25)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which basic design element marks a position in space, has no length, width, or depth, and is treated as the generator behind every architectural form?
o: Line
Point
Plane
Volume
n: Answer: C — A point marks a position in space with no dimension, and is the primitive generator of line, plane, and volume. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q26)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term, in architectural graphics and form theory, names the degree of stability and visual concentration a form conveys, based on its shape, orientation, and relation to the ground plane?
o: Visual Inertia
Surface Articulation
Visual Scale
Volumetric Proportion
n: Answer: B — Visual inertia describes a form's degree of stability/concentration, based on its shape, orientation, and relation to the ground. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q27)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: When part of a basic geometric form's volume is removed while its overall formal identity remains intact, what kind of transformation is this?
o: Dimensional Transformation
Subtractive Transformation
Parametric Transformation
Additive Transformation
n: Answer: C — Removing volume from a primary solid while its overall identity remains recognizable is a subtractive transformation. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q28)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Raising a base plane above the surrounding ground creates a distinct zone. What kind of relationship, psychologically and visually, does this establish between the raised plane and the lower ground around it?
o: Total spatial continuity with no visual boundary
An unstable, weak architectural zone
A clear sense of detachment, prominence, and territorial domain
A highly introverted, hidden pocket of space
n: Answer: B — An elevated plane visually and psychologically separates itself, creating a sense of prominence, detachment, and territory. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q29)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: By contrast, what effect does depressing a base plane below the surrounding grade produce?
o: It acts as a monumental marker visible from great distances
It maximizes structural tension across the site
It forms an introverted, and localized field of space that feels enclosed and distinct
It eliminates social activities in the surrounding
n: Answer: D — A depressed plane forms an introverted, sheltered field of space distinct from — but continuous with — the surrounding ground. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q30)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term names the recognizable outline or surface configuration of a form — the main way we identify and tell apart three-dimensional volumes?
o: Size
Shape
Texture
Position
n: Answer: C — Shape is the characteristic outline/contour that lets us identify and distinguish a form. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q31)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Rotating a triangle about its vertical apex axis generates which three-dimensional solid?
o: Sphere
Cylinder
Cone
Pyramid
n: Answer: B — Rotating a triangle about its vertical apex axis sweeps out a cone. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q32)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which term, often rendered as 'spirit of the place,' names the distinctive character a location carries because of its geography, history, and built form?
o: Zeitgeist
Partis
Genius Loci
Parti Pris
n: Answer: D — 'Genius loci,' Latin for 'spirit of place,' describes the unique character rooted in a site's geography, history, and form. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q33)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does a highly polished, mirror-like floor finish typically alter how occupants perceive a lobby's spatial dimensions?
o: It gives an optical illusion of extra vertical depth by reflecting the ceiling, making the room seem taller than it actually is.
It makes the space read as darker and more cramped than it really is.
It draws attention to the form itself, sharpening the perception of its three-dimensional geometry.
It visually stabilizes heavy columns by soaking up ambient light.
n: Answer: D — A polished reflective floor mirrors the ceiling plane, creating an illusion of greater vertical height. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q34)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In color theory, adding which neutral to a pure hue produces a 'tone'?
o: By mixing two secondary colors together
By adding grey to a pure hue
By adding black to a pure hue
By adding white to a pure hue
n: Answer: C — In color theory a tone is produced by adding grey (a mix of black and white) to a pure hue. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q35)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the name for a hue that has been darkened by mixing in black, lowering its value below that of the pure parent color?
o: Tint
Shade
Tone
Intensity
n: Answer: C — A shade is a hue mixed with black, which lowers its value and darkens it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q36)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which color has been shown clinically to reduce blood pressure and respiration rate, producing a calm, sociofugal environment well suited to healthcare recovery spaces?
o: Low-value Yellow
Low-chroma Blue
High-saturation Orange
High-value Red
n: Answer: B — Low-chroma/desaturated blue is documented to calm the nervous system, lowering blood pressure and respiration — useful in healing environments. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q37)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: For an interior scheme built on a split-complementary harmony anchored by yellow, which two other hues round out the palette?
o: Green and Orange
Red and Blue
Red-Violet and Blue-Violet
Violet and Blue-Violet
n: Answer: B — Yellow's complement is violet; a split-complementary scheme pairs yellow with the two hues flanking violet — red-violet and blue-violet. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q38)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Selecting two hues sitting directly across from each other on a 12-part color wheel produces which type of harmony?
o: Monochromatic Harmony
Triadic Harmony
Analogous Harmony
Complementary Harmony
n: Answer: C — Complementary harmony pairs hues directly opposite each other on the color wheel. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q39)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In commercial kitchen planning, which ergonomic path connecting the sink, refrigerator, and range is treated as the essential blueprint for efficient workflow?
o: The Circulation Spine
The Linear Assembly
The Work Triangle
The Concentric Ring
n: Answer: B — The Work Triangle links the sink, refrigerator, and range/stove for efficient kitchen circulation. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q40)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In commercial kitchen layout, how much clearance should separate two facing rows of low cabinets or appliances so two cooks can work back-to-back with oven doors open?
o: 900 mm
n: Answer: C — Commercial kitchen guidelines call for roughly 1500 mm between facing equipment rows when staff must pass back-to-back with oven doors open. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q41)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: For a secondary residential corridor, what is the minimum clearance width so two average adults can pass each other without turning sideways?
o: 900 mm
n: Answer: B — Building/space-planning standards set about 1200 mm as the minimum secondary corridor width for two people to pass comfortably. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q42)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What core distinction separates 'personal space' from 'territoriality' in environmental psychology?
o: Personal space is a fixed geographic area, while territoriality is the portable bubble that moves with a person.
Personal space is an invisible zone that travels with a person, while territoriality is a fixed area someone claims as their own.
Personal space needs a legal deed, while territoriality does not.
Personal space is relevant only to interiors, while territoriality applies only to urban planning.
n: Answer: D — Personal space is a portable psychological 'bubble' that travels with a person, while territoriality is a fixed area someone claims and defends. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q43)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Alan Westin described four states of privacy. Which one names being physically present in a public crowd — a plaza or café — yet free from being singled out or watched because one blends into the surroundings?
o: Anonymity
Solitude
Reserve
Intimacy
n: Answer: C — Alan Westin's 'anonymity' describes being unidentified and unobserved while present in a public crowd. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q44)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Universal-design guidance and codes such as BP 344 call for strong color contrast between doors, wayfinding signage, and adjoining walls. What is this contrast mainly meant to achieve?
o: Matching the strict minimalist lines associated with the International Style.
Cutting the cost of interior graphic branding.
Damping noise reflections along public evacuation routes.
Helping people with low vision follow paths of travel and locate emergency exits through clear visual cues.
n: Answer: D — High-contrast signage/door colors under codes like BP 344 help low-vision users identify paths of travel and exits. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q45)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How might an interior architect use color choices in a workspace to shape thermal comfort and cut down on energy consumption?
o: Color has no bearing at all on how someone perceives a room's temperature.
By using cool tones to lower the perceived temperature in hot tropical settings.
By using glossy neon paint to physically hold cool air against the wall surface.
By painting rooms bright pink to block HVAC drafts.
n: Answer: B — Cool colors (blues/greens) can lower a room's perceived temperature, helping thermal comfort in hot climates. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q46)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: To design a fast-casual restaurant's dining area for quick customer turnover and strong appetite stimulation, which color approach should dominate?
o: Solid monochrome blacks and charcoal grays meant to slow movement.
Low-saturation, low-chroma tones that engage the autonomic nervous system to sharpen appetite while quietly encouraging restlessness against overstaying.
Highly saturated colors that stimulate appetite while inducing mild restlessness that speeds up turnover.
Soft pastel lavenders and muted sky blues meant to spark hunger and restlessness.
n: Answer: A — High-saturation warm colors stimulate appetite while producing mild restlessness, encouraging quick turnover in fast-casual dining. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q47)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Looking at Ancient Egypt's architectural timeline, what structural shift marks the move from Old Kingdom to New Kingdom royal burial practices?
o: Adopting Roman-style concrete vaulting inside temple layouts.
Trading open-air limestone colonnades for brick ziggurat platforms.
Abandoning stone masonry entirely in favor of monumental timber post-and-lintel framing.
A shift away from prominent above-ground monuments toward hidden, rock-cut tombs meant to deter looting.
n: Answer: D — Egyptian royal burials shifted from visible Old Kingdom pyramids to hidden, rock-cut New Kingdom tombs (Valley of the Kings) to deter raiders. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q48)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: The move from classical Greek to Roman architecture marked a huge shift in structural engineering. What breakthrough made that leap possible?
o: The invention of high-tensile steel alloys.
Trading marble columns for lightweight bamboo framing.
Moving beyond a purely trabeated system to opus caementicium and the true arch.
Moving from the semi-circular arch and barrel vault toward the pointed arch and ribbed vault.
n: Answer: B — Rome's development of opus caementicium (concrete) and the true arch freed architecture from the strictly post-and-lintel Greek trabeated system. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q49)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace, built for London's 1851 Great Exhibition, is regarded as a turning point on the architectural timeline. Why?
o: It brought the first publicly operating electric elevator into use.
It was the first public building since antiquity to use hand-carved classical marble orders.
It effectively ended urban planning regulation across Europe.
It showed that huge structures could be assembled quickly from modular, prefabricated iron and glass.
n: Answer: C — The Crystal Palace proved that a massive building could be rapidly assembled from prefabricated, modular iron-and-glass components. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q50)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Put these historical design movements in the correct chronological order along the architectural timeline.
o: Baroque → Gothic → Renaissance → Modernism → Art Nouveau
Gothic → Renaissance → Baroque → Art Nouveau → Modernism
Renaissance → Gothic → Baroque → Modernism → Art Nouveau
Gothic → Baroque → Renaissance → Art Nouveau → Modernism
n: Answer: B — The correct historical order is Gothic → Renaissance → Baroque → Art Nouveau → Modernism. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q51)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In his 1896 essay 'The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered,' Louis Sullivan coined 'form follows function.' Which architectural device did he use to express a skyscraper's three-part division, echoing a classical column?
o: A clear tripartite reading of base, shaft, and crowning cornice.
An unbroken glass skin exposing the structural core and building systems.
A decorative, non-structural steel curtain wall running across every intermediate floor.
A system of buttresses that thin out as the building rises.
n: Answer: B — Sullivan described the skyscraper's tripartite division — base, shaft, and cornice/top — echoing a classical column. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q52)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Le Corbusier's 'Five Points of Architecture' broke sharply from traditional load-bearing masonry. Which structural element made both the 'free plan' and the 'free façade' possible?
o: A central masonry core carrying every lateral and gravity load.
Heavy timber post-and-beam joinery removing any need for deep foundations.
Load-bearing reinforced concrete walls running around the perimeter.
Pilotis lifting the building volume, paired with an internal reinforced-concrete column grid and cantilevered slabs.
n: Answer: B — Pilotis, an internal reinforced-concrete column grid, and cantilevered slabs free both the plan and facade from load-bearing walls. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q53)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Frank Lloyd Wright coined 'Organic Architecture.' Which choice best captures how that idea shows up in his Fallingwater (the Kaufmann House)?
o: A perfectly circular plan avoiding harsh, artificial right angles.
Mimicking biological structures such as skeletons and leaf veins within the structural frame.
Concrete terraces blended into the site's topography, echoing the natural rock ledges above the waterfall.
An insistence on biodegradable, locally sourced materials so the building would eventually decompose.
n: Answer: C — Fallingwater's cantilevered concrete terraces echo the natural rock ledges of the site, embodying Wright's organic architecture. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q54)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Walter Gropius's Bauhaus building in Dessau is a landmark of the International Style. Which strategy gave the workshop wing its weightless, transparent look?
o: An unbroken glass curtain wall set independent of a recessed structural grid.
Thick, load-bearing brick walls punctuated by small, rhythmic windows.
A structure built entirely of tensile fabric membranes and steel cables.
An asymmetrical row of heavy stone pilasters flanking the entrance.
n: Answer: A — Gropius wrapped the Dessau workshop wing in a continuous glass curtain wall set free of the recessed structural grid, expressing weightlessness. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q55)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Mies van der Rohe's 'less is more' reached its corporate peak in the Seagram Building. To express the internal steel frame on the exterior while meeting fire code, what solution did he use?
o: A curtain wall cast entirely of raw, board-formed concrete.
Leaving the structural steel columns fully exposed with no fireproofing at all.
Non-structural bronze I-beam mullions applied to the exterior to echo the structural rhythm.
A structural glass-fin system that removed the need for vertical metal mullions.
n: Answer: B — Fire codes required Mies to fireproof the Seagram Building's real steel frame, so he applied non-structural bronze I-beam mullions to express structural rhythm. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q56)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Alvar Aalto's Paimio Sanatorium broke from the rigid orthogonal rationalism common in early Central European modernism. How did he weave humanistic and psychological concerns into the design?

With monumental, symmetrical neoclassical façades meant to convey civic authority.

Delirious New York

Burying every structural and mechanical system inside a thick stone-clad shell to fit the Parisian context.
Exposing and color-coding the steel frame and mechanical/electrical/plumbing systems right on the exterior.

q: Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation in Marseille is widely seen as Brutalism's founding project. What material reality during its construction gave the movement its name?

Unpolished steel beams left exposed to rust with time.
The demolition of historic neighborhoods through aggressive eminent-domain tactics.
Rough concrete left raw straight from the timber formwork — what the French called 'béton brut.'

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics

Sticking closely to the rigid, right-angled grids favored by the International Style.
Relying exclusively on traditional thatched roofs supported by local bamboo.
Sculptural reinforced-concrete curves drawn from Brazil's landscape.

A sharp line separating the ground plaza from the building façade using abrupt material changes.
An efficient, modular field of identical triangular panels suited to mass production.
An echo of traditional Islamic mud-brick fortification logic.

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics

The Glass House sits on high steel stilts above a floodplain, while the Farnsworth House rests directly on a solid concrete foundation.
The Glass House relies on load-bearing stone arches, while the Farnsworth House relies on a steel space frame.

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics

As biological organisms with a fixed structural spine hosting replaceable, plug-in modules.
As mobile, aerodynamic vehicles able to physically relocate across cities via mechanical tracks.
As static monuments meant to resist all social or technological change.

Pilotis

A cross-shaped void cut into a raw concrete altar wall to let in natural light.

A soaring, gold-leafed Gothic spire.
A working exterior elevator cage painted bright orange.
A row of raw, unpolished concrete columns left exposed to the weather.

Trading curved forms for intersecting flat, orthogonal triangles.
Using AI to generate thousands of random, irregular forms.

A transcription of a traditional German symphony's sound wave.
An echo of the military trench routes from the Franco-Prussian War.

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics

Its construction on illegal municipal parkland without proper zoning.
Deterioration of the capsule structure from unreplaced modules, rusted joints, burst pipes, and hazardous asbestos.

A subterranean cavern meant to shield passengers from noise.
The rigid mechanical efficiency of a factory assembly line.
A historic Gothic cathedral spire adapted to an industrial airfield.

An exterior skin made entirely of unpainted corrugated steel panels.

Fast, structurally sound, low-cost disaster-relief housing and temporary shelters for refugees and disaster victims.
Cheap, automated luxury hotels for mid-income travelers worldwide.

Ornament applied as shallow plaster relief onto conventional brick bearing walls.
Eliminating structural metal entirely in favor of hand-carved local timber joinery.
Hiding structural elements behind heavy concrete slabs to leave room for canvas paintings.

Tripartite corporate stacking, classical column modules, and structural concealment.
