Habagat
Timog
n: Answer: B — The Amihan is the cool, dry northeast wind that dominates the Philippines from roughly November to February. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q103)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: From June through October, which wind dominates the Philippine climate, blowing from the southwest and carrying heavy, moisture-laden monsoon air?
o: Salatan
Timog
Habagat
Amihan
n: Answer: A — The Habagat is the moist southwest monsoon wind that dominates from about June to October. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q104)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In tropical building physics, why does high relative humidity make an interior feel hotter than the thermometer reading alone would suggest?
o: High humidity increases the speed of radiant heat transfer from walls to skin
It drops the oxygen content of the room, forcing blood pressure to spike
High humidity causes air molecules to compress, generating friction heat
High humidity stops sweat from drying, trapping body heat.
n: Answer: D — High humidity slows sweat evaporation, trapping body heat and making the same temperature feel hotter. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q105)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term describes dense cities like Manila running 2°C to 5°C warmer than nearby rural fields, driven by dark asphalt, concrete mass, and sparse greenery?
o: Urban Heat Island Effect
Atmospheric Inversion
Microclimate Stratification
Greenhouse Concentricity
n: Answer: C — The Urban Heat Island Effect describes dense cities running measurably warmer than surrounding rural land due to dark, hard surfaces. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q106)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In tropical climates, what functional problem does a very small diurnal temperature range (the gap between daytime high and nighttime low) create?
o: It eliminates wind movement across the landscape entirely.
Warm nighttime air fails to purge the solar heat that heavy concrete walls absorbed during the day.
It causes rapid cracking in exterior timber assemblies.
It causes daily solar power output to drop.
n: Answer: A — A small diurnal range means nights don't cool enough to flush the solar heat that concrete/masonry walls absorbed during the day. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q107)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which Philippine wind pattern describes a daily local cycle in which cool ocean air moves inland during the afternoon to replace rising hot air over land?
o: Katabatic Mountain Wind
Cyclonic Monsoon Core
Sea Breeze (Ambon)
Land Breeze (Tungkasan)
n: Answer: B — A sea breeze is the daily cycle where cooler ocean air moves inland in the afternoon as land air heats and rises. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q108)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: To stay as cool as possible in Philippine heat, along which direction should a building's long axis run so its largest walls avoid direct morning and afternoon sun?
o: East-to-West
Angled diagonally at 45 degrees
North-to-South
Perpendicular to the closest coastline
n: Answer: A — Stretching a building's long axis East-to-West minimizes the exposed wall area facing the intense low-angle morning/afternoon sun. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q109)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which building façades in the Philippines take the most intense low-angle solar heat, making them hardest to shade with simple horizontal overhangs?
o: North and South facades
Northeast and Southwest facades
Only the true North façade
East and West facades
n: Answer: B — East and West facades receive intense, low-angle sun that horizontal overhangs (better suited to high-angle sun) can't easily block. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q110)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: For shading a true north- or south-facing window from high-angle noon sun in the Philippines, which external device works best?
o: Eggcrate shading panels painted pitch black
Deep horizontal overhangs or canopy slabs
Vertical louvers or vertical fins
Double-pane reflective tinted glass mirroring
n: Answer: B — Deep horizontal overhangs/canopies are most effective at blocking the high-angle noon sun typical on North/South facades. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q111)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which shading-device layout best blocks the low-angle morning and afternoon sun striking east and west façades?
o: Eggcrate shading panels painted pitch black
Double-pane reflective tinted glass mirroring
Vertical louvers or vertical fins
Deep horizontal overhangs or canopy slabs
n: Answer: A — Vertical louvers or fins are best suited to block the low, raking morning/afternoon sun on East/West facades. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q112)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: If a building has a massive, unshaded concrete roof slab in a tropical climate, what thermal problem shows up in the late evening?
o: Heat absorbed during the day radiates back down from the concrete slab at night.
The roof suddenly turns freezing cold, causing internal condensation.
The roof slab physically deflects downward from structural contraction.
Cross-ventilation velocity drops off entirely.
n: Answer: C — A massive unshaded concrete roof stores solar heat during the day and re-radiates it downward into the interior at night. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q113)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which roof pitch best sheds heavy monsoon rain quickly in a tropical building while letting hot air pool near the peak, away from occupants?
o: Low-angle sawtooth roof facing due West
Completely flat roof with deep concrete parapet walls
Steeply pitched roof with generous overhanging eaves
Mono-sloped roof sloping down toward the primary windward inlet
n: Answer: C — A steep roof pitch with generous eaves sheds heavy monsoon rain fast while letting hot air rise and pool near the peak, away from occupants. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q114)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the main job of a 'breeze block' or 'breeze sole' screen wall in a tropical building envelope?
o: To act as a load-bearing column system for multi-story towers.
To shade the sun while blocking breezes from passing through.
To cut direct solar glare while still letting natural air currents pass through.
To increase heat gain while letting air pass through.
n: Answer: C — Breeze blocks perforate a wall to cut direct glare while still letting natural airflow pass through. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q115)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In solar geometry, what does 'azimuth' refer to?
o: The vertical angle of the sun above the flat horizon.
The vertical distance of the sun measured along the horizon.
The thickness of the atmospheric ozone layer over a site.
The horizontal angular position of the sun measured along the horizon.
n: Answer: D — Azimuth is the sun's horizontal angular position measured along the horizon; altitude is its vertical angle. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q116)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: To cut heat transfer into a building's interior, what U-value should exterior wall insulation aim for?
o: A U-value of exactly 1.0
U-value has no impact on tropical heat transfers
A very high U-value
A low U-value, indicating high resistance to heat flow
n: Answer: B — Good insulation should have a low U-value, meaning high resistance to heat flow. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q117)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why should highly reflective, glossy exterior finishes be used cautiously in dense Philippine urban areas?
o: They absorb too much moisture during typhoons.
They pull intense heat directly into neighboring structures.
They bounce solar glare and heat onto neighbors, creating thermal problems for them.
They attract insects during monsoon season.
n: Answer: C — Highly reflective finishes can bounce intense solar glare and heat onto neighboring buildings and streets. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q118)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What aerodynamic principle explains air speeding up as wind is forced through a narrowed opening within a building layout?
o: The Stack Effect
The Venturi Effect
The Doppler Shift
Archimedes' Principle
n: Answer: B — The Venturi Effect explains why air speeds up when forced through a narrowed opening. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q119)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: To maximize the speed and volume of natural cross-ventilation through a room, how should the windward inlet size relate to the leeward outlet?
o: An inlet equal to or smaller than the outlet creates a pressure difference that speeds up indoor airflow.
Both openings must sit at exactly the same height on the same wall.
The outlet window must face directly toward the floor.
An inlet equal to or larger than the outlet creates a pressure difference that speeds up indoor airflow.
n: Answer: A — Sizing the inlet smaller than the outlet creates a pressure differential (like a nozzle) that speeds up indoor air movement. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q120)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which passive ventilation strategy relies on density differences, where warm indoor air rises and exits through high roof vents, drawing cooler air in through low wall inlets?
o: The Venturi Effect
Archimedes' Principle
The Doppler Shift
The Stack Effect
n: Answer: A — The stack effect relies on warm, buoyant air rising and exiting high vents, drawing cooler air in through low openings. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q121)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which window type opens to 100% of its area for ventilation while still shedding tropical rain?
o: Jalousie windows
hopper windows
Casement windows
Fixed glass curtain walls
n: Answer: C — Jalousie windows open to nearly 100% of their area while their angled glass slats still shed rain. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q122)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What landscape feature, placed upwind of a building's main air inlet, can cool incoming air currents?
o: A large asphalt parking lot with no tree cover.
Densely planted shrubs placed just below the openings.
A lawn paired with an open water feature to support localized evaporative cooling.
A hedge acting as a natural fence.
n: Answer: D — A water feature or lawn placed upwind of an inlet cools incoming air through evaporative cooling. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q123)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What passive-cooling benefit do wide, overhanging open-air verandas provide in a tropical resort design?
o: They extend the building's life by keeping exterior materials from decaying.
They shade the main perimeter walls from direct solar heat while sheltering them from rain.
They fully seal the core building off from storm-wind dynamics.
They serve as heavy structural counterweights against severe seismic movement.
n: Answer: B — Wide overhanging verandas shade a building's perimeter walls from direct sun while sheltering them from rain. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q124)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: To lower a window's solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) without adding external shading, what glass technology should an architect specify?
o: Clear 6mm single-pane float glass
Low-Emissivity reflective double-glazed units
Wire-reinforced clear fire-rated glass
High-transparency structural acoustic glass panels
n: Answer: D — Low-Emissivity, reflective double-glazed units reduce a window's solar heat gain coefficient without needing external shading. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q125)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: The traditional Bahay Kubo is a textbook example of tropical passive design. What material choice keeps the structure from storing heat?
o: Massive load-bearing coral stone blocks
Lightweight, porous organic materials that have low thermal mass
Poured reinforced concrete frames clad in volcanic tuff panels
Elevated on stilts and lightweight wooden panels to absorb heat
n: Answer: B — The Bahay Kubo's light, porous natural materials (bamboo, nipa) have low thermal mass, so the structure doesn't store heat. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q126)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why is the floor plane of a traditional Bahay Kubo raised on wooden stilts above the ground?
o: To protect occupants from flooding and pests.
To give a defensible vantage point during local tribal conflicts.
To stiffen the roof trusses structurally during typhoons.
To cut the building off entirely from cross-ventilation currents.
n: Answer: A — Elevating the Bahay Kubo on stilts protects occupants and the structure from floodwater and ground pests. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q127)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In a Spanish-colonial Bahay na Bato, which spatial and structural feature merges the lightweight, climate-conscious logic of the Bahay Kubo with heavy European stone construction?
o: A heavy stone upper floor resting on top of a lightweight bamboo ground floor
A heavy masonry ground floor topped by a timber upper residential story
The elimination of all windows on the upper residential levels
A building envelope constructed entirely out of imported sheet metal
n: Answer: B — The Bahay na Bato pairs a heavy masonry ground floor with a lighter timber upper residential story. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q128)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What structural element in a Bahay na Bato is a delicate, pierced wooden screen set just below the ceiling line, letting hot air pass freely between rooms?
o: Volada
Ventanilla
Zaguan
Calado
n: Answer: A — The calado is a pierced wooden screen near the ceiling that lets hot air circulate freely between rooms. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q129)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What function do the ventanilla sliding panels beneath the main windowsills serve in a Bahay na Bato?
o: Acting as escape hatches during structural collapse.
Allowing low-level cross-ventilation to sweep across the floor plane.
Serving a decorative role while still letting air pass through.
Letting hot air pass freely between rooms.
n: Answer: A — Ventanilla sliding panels beneath the windowsill admit low-level cross-ventilation across the floor where occupants sit. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q130)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Translucent capiz shells were used in Bahay na Bato window sashes instead of heavy glass. What was their main advantage in tropical design?
o: They actively lower the relative humidity of incoming air
They filter diffused indoor light while holding up against typhoon wind
They are completely soundproof and block street noise
They act as a firewall to block the spread of municipal fires
n: Answer: B — Capiz shell panes diffuse soft interior light while remaining durable enough to withstand typhoon winds. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q131)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: On a site map, what does it mean when contour lines are drawn very close together?
o: A high flood risk zone
A perfectly flat open field
An underground utility pipeline
A steep slope or cliff
n: Answer: B — Closely spaced contour lines indicate a steep slope or cliff. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q132)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: During site analysis, what does soil bearing capacity tell an architect?
o: The percentage of organic compost inside the dirt
How much weight the soil can safely support before a building foundation sinks
How much water the soil can hold during a heavy storm
The required depth of the foundation of the building
n: Answer: D — Soil bearing capacity tells an architect how much load the ground can safely carry before a foundation sinks. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q133)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the goal of a 'cut and fill' strategy in site grading?
o: Cutting down all trees and replacing them with gravel fill
Balancing the soil level to prevent possible soil erosion or landslide
Digging deep trenches to look for hidden historic artifacts
Minimizing the cost of hauling soil away or buying new soil
n: Answer: B — Cut-and-fill grading balances excavated and needed soil on site, minimizing the cost of hauling material away or importing it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q134)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is a 'bioswale' within sustainable site planning?
o: A plastic tank buried underground to store drinking water
A shallow, landscaped ditch filled with plants designed to naturally capture, slow down, and filter stormwater runoff
A mechanical pump used to clear sewage
A drainage system or a surface trench drain to protect properties from flooding and erosion by safely channeling rainwater
n: Answer: D — A bioswale is a shallow, planted depression designed to capture, slow, and filter stormwater runoff. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q135)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What design challenge does a 'high water table' present to an architect?
o: Shallow groundwater makes basements highly prone to flooding.
A high water table is unsafe and makes excavating soil more difficult.
The building must be constructed of lightweight timber frames.
The air over the site stays completely dry year-round.
n: Answer: B — A high water table means shallow groundwater, making basements especially prone to flooding and requiring waterproofing. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q136)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In site design, how does a 'vista' differ from a 'panorama'?
o: There is no difference; they are identical terms
A vista can only be seen at night, while a panorama is seen by day
A vista is a wide, 360-degree unblocked view, while a panorama is hidden
A vista is a framed view, while a panorama is a wide, open view in all directions
n: Answer: B — A vista is a framed, directed view (often along an axis), while a panorama is a wide, open view in all directions. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q137)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why is it recommended to lay out outdoor parking rows north-to-south rather than east-to-west?
o: It lets more cars fit into a single lot layout.
It aligns vehicles with the Earth's magnetic field to prevent battery drain.
It is cheaper and easier for drivers to park.
It cuts down the time vehicles sit exposed to low-angle sun, keeping them cooler.
n: Answer: A — Orienting parking rows North–South limits how long parked cars sit exposed to the low, direct East/West sun, keeping them cooler. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q138)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In sustainable landscape architecture, why are native plants generally preferred over imported exotic species?
o: Native plants grow to the same height as the building roof line
Native plants are completely immune to direct solar radiation
Native plants look grows faster than exotic plants
Native plants are significantly less water, fertilizers, and maintenance
n: Answer: A — Native plants are adapted to local conditions and typically need far less water, fertilizer, and maintenance than exotic species. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q139)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which site element best blocks loud traffic noise from a nearby highway from reaching a residential building?
o: Painting the building exterior bright reflective white.
An earth berm paired with a thick layer of dense shrubs and trees.
A wide lawn with no trees, paired with an espalier concrete fence.
A thin chain-link fence.
n: Answer: C — An earth berm combined with dense shrubs and trees is an effective passive barrier against highway traffic noise. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q140)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In site analysis, what does 'microclimate' mean?
o: A localized area where climate factors — temperature, humidity, wind, rainfall — differ noticeably from the surrounding regional climate.
The localized climate of a broader regional area spanning tens to hundreds of kilometers.
A weather forecast that updates every five minutes.
The localized conditions of one specific small site, shaped by its topography, trees, water features, and surrounding structures.
n: Answer: A — A microclimate is a localized area whose temperature, humidity, wind, or rainfall differs notably from the surrounding regional climate. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q141)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the main purpose of conducting a 'site inventory' early in a project?
o: To create a checklist of all existing physical features of the site
To calculate the final rental price of the building spaces
To choose the existing elements of the site and check the cost of it
To order the final building construction materials
n: Answer: C — A site inventory catalogs all existing physical features of a site as a baseline before design begins. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q142)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why is stripping every mature tree from a sloped site dangerous for the surrounding development?
o: It drops the water table too quickly.
Removing trees damages soil quality and weakens bearing capacity, leading to erosion and landslides.
Tree roots hold soil together and absorb rainwater; removing them raises the risk of severe erosion and landslides during storms.
It violates the local ecosystem.
n: Answer: B — Mature tree roots stabilize slope soil and absorb rainwater; removing them raises the risk of erosion and landslides. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q143)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In landscape design, what is an 'earth berm'?
o: A soil used to collect rainwater
A decorative stone fountain
A deep trench used to drain sewage
A raised, intentional mound of soil
n: Answer: D — An earth berm is a raised, intentionally shaped mound of soil used for screening, shading, or noise control. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q144)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the main design advantage of planting deciduous trees for solar shading along a building's south-facing side?
o: They provide food and shelter for wildlife, boost biodiversity, and help control erosion.
They block 100% of wind year-round.
They function as natural windbreaks and privacy screens, control erosion, and shelter birds and mammals.
They provide dense shade in hot summer months but drop their leaves in cold seasons, letting sunlight through and warming the building.
n: Answer: D — Deciduous trees shade a south facade in summer heat and drop their leaves in winter, letting sunlight through when it's wanted. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q145)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term describes a broad, paved public walkway along a scenic waterfront, beach, or riverbank, meant for leisurely strolling?
o: Cul-de-sac
Esplanade
Alleyway
Pleached walkway
n: Answer: B — An esplanade is a broad, paved public walkway along a waterfront meant for leisurely strolling. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q146)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What outdoor structure is an open timber frame of columns and crossbeams, often covered in climbing vines, used to frame a garden path or create shaded seating?
o: Pergola
Vestibule
Trellis
Gazebo
n: Answer: A — A pergola is an open timber framework of posts and cross-beams, often planted with vines, that frames a path or shaded seating area. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q147)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which landscape element is a continuous, tightly packed row of shrubs or small trees forming a living wall to mark boundaries or block views?
o: Hedge
Bushes
Fence line
Parterre
n: Answer: B — A hedge is a dense, continuous planted row that forms a living wall marking boundaries or screening views. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q148)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How do 'hardscape' and 'softscape' differ in landscape architecture?
o: Hardscape comprises living elements, while softscape comprises all non-living elements
Hardscape is built by architects, while softscape is managed only by civil engineers
Hardscape comprises non-living elements, while softscape comprises all living plant materials
Hardscape handles water systems, while softscape handles lighting layouts
n: Answer: A — Hardscape refers to non-living built elements (paving, walls), while softscape refers to living plant materials. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q149)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Ebenezer Howard introduced the Garden City concept in 1898. What was its core layout?
o: A giant industrial complex with housing placed directly on its roofs.
Self-contained, walkable towns surrounded by a greenbelt.
An endless line of skyscrapers strung along a greenbelt.
A grid dedicated entirely to automobile traffic with no parks.
n: Answer: D — Howard's Garden City model proposed self-contained, walkable towns encircled by a protective greenbelt. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q150)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the primary aim of Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) in modern urban planning?
o: To move all public transit networks completely underground.
To focus on public transit in a way that spreads future development further from existing districts.
To build massive highways letting cars travel across cities faster.
To cluster high-density housing, offices, and shops within short walking distance of transit hubs.
n: Answer: B — Transit-Oriented Development clusters dense housing, offices, and retail within easy walking distance of transit hubs. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q151)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does 'urban sprawl' refer to?
o: The planting of forests inside a downtown commercial core
The conversion of old factories into public libraries
The uncontrolled, uncoordinated outward growth of a city
The vertical growth of a city using high-rise skyscrapers
n: Answer: C — Urban sprawl describes the uncontrolled, low-density, outward expansion of a city. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q152)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which neighborhood design layout does the 'New Urbanism' movement champion?
o: Sprawling, car-dependent cul-de-sacs with large front lawns.
Walkable, human-scaled neighborhoods.
Moving all residential communities into high-altitude mountain zones.
Mega-blocks separated by twelve-lane highways.
n: Answer: B — New Urbanism promotes walkable, human-scaled neighborhoods in place of car-dependent sprawl. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q153)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does the Concentric Zone Model describe a city's growth?
o: Land use organized in pie-shaped sectors or wedges growing outward along major transportation corridors.
Pie-shaped slices growing outward along major transit routes.
A city growing around several independent focal points or specialized hubs.
Target-like concentric rings radiating outward from a single central business district.
n: Answer: B — The Concentric Zone Model (Burgess) describes a city as a series of rings expanding outward from a central business district. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q154)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: By contrast, how does the Sector Model (Hoyt Model) map out urban land use?
o: Land use organized in pie-shaped sectors or wedges growing outward along major transportation corridors.
A city growing around several independent focal points or specialized hubs.
Target-like concentric rings radiating outward from a single central business district.
Pie-shaped slices growing outward along major transit routes.
n: Answer: C — The Sector Model (Hoyt) describes land use radiating outward in pie-shaped wedges along transportation corridors. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q155)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: The 'Multiple Nuclei Model' describes modern metropolitan growth around what basic claim?
o: Target-like concentric rings radiating outward from a single central business district.
A city growing around several independent focal points or specialized hubs.
Pie-shaped slices growing outward along major transit routes.
Land use organized in pie-shaped sectors or wedges growing outward along major transportation corridors.
n: Answer: D — The Multiple Nuclei Model holds that cities grow around several independent, specialized focal points rather than one center. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q156)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does 'gentrification' mean in an urban context?
o: Planting trees along public highway medians.
Wealthier residents moving into a lower-income neighborhood, pushing up property values and rents and often displacing the original community.
Structurally reinforcing old bridges against earthquakes.
Forced or coerced displacement of people from their homes, typically due to war, violence, or natural disaster.
n: Answer: B — Gentrification is the influx of wealthier residents into a lower-income neighborhood, raising costs and often displacing the original community. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q157)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What defines a 'mega-city'?
o: A continuous urban metropolitan area with a total population exceeding 10 million people
A continuous urban metropolitan area with a total population exceeding 100 thousand people
A continuous urban metropolitan area with a total population exceeding 100 million people
A continuous urban metropolitan area with a total population exceeding 1 million people
n: Answer: C — A megacity is a continuous metropolitan area with a population exceeding 10 million. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q158)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does a 'greenbelt' do in metropolitan planning?
o: Pipe recycled water to protect parks and green spaces.
Serve as a lawn placed in front of corporate office buildings.
Mark bicycle lanes on roads with a line of green paint.
Form a protected ring of open space that contains urban sprawl and preserves natural habitat.
n: Answer: D — A greenbelt is a protected ring of open land encircling a city to contain sprawl and preserve natural habitat. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q159)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What criticism was often leveled at mid-20th-century Urban Renewal programs focused on total slum clearance?
o: They spent too little on decorative monuments.
Wealthier residents moved in, pushing up property values and rents and displacing the original community.
Forced or coerced displacement of people from their homes, typically due to war, violence, or natural disaster.
They frequently demolished historic neighborhoods and displaced low-income communities without offering proper housing alternatives.
n: Answer: B — Mid-century Urban Renewal was criticized for demolishing historic, low-income neighborhoods without providing adequate replacement housing. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q160)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is 'urban blight' or 'urban decay'?
o: The functional deterioration, abandonment, and economic decline of inner-city buildings and infrastructure.
Demolishing historic neighborhoods and displacing low-income communities without proper housing alternatives.
Converting old, abandoned urban assets into new public amenities like parks, markets, and cultural hubs.
A design trend favoring raw, unpolished concrete façades.
n: Answer: C — Urban blight/decay refers to the functional deterioration, abandonment, and economic decline of inner-city buildings and infrastructure. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q161)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In urban planning maps, how is residential density typically measured and expressed?
o: The total weight of residential buildings divided by road lengths
The number of individual dwelling units per unit of land area
The number of windows per building facade
The number of cars parked along a single residential street
n: Answer: B — Residential density is expressed as the number of dwelling units per unit of land area. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q162)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is a 'Planned Unit Development' (PUD)?
o: An urban park made entirely of identical playground equipment.
A mechanical engineering blueprint for municipal water treatment facilities.
A standard housing community where every lot follows identical setback distances.
A flexible master-planned category allowing mixed uses, varied housing types, and unique setbacks on one large parcel, bypassing rigid zoning blocks.
n: Answer: B — A Planned Unit Development is a flexible master-planned zoning category allowing mixed uses and housing types on one large parcel. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q163)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the fundamental difference between 'land use' and 'zoning'?
o: Land use is handled by private developers, while zoning is handled only by structural engineers.
Land use applies to rural areas, while zoning applies strictly to inner-city downtown blocks.
There is no difference; the two terms are legally identical.
Land use records what is currently happening on the ground, while zoning is the legal tool and set of rules dictating what can be built there going forward.
n: Answer: A — Land use describes what is actually on the ground now; zoning is the legal regulation controlling what may be built there. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q164)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In Kevin Lynch's *Image of the City*, what term names strategic focal points or busy gathering spots where major paths cross, such as a central train station or a bustling square?
o: Districts
Nodes
Landmarks
Edges
n: Answer: C — Kevin Lynch's 'nodes' are strategic, busy focal points, such as where major paths intersect. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q165)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: According to Kevin Lynch, what is an 'edge' in a person's mental map of a city?
o: A major highway that pedestrians use to travel across town
A towering skyscraper visible from any point in the city
A linear boundary that acts as a barrier or structural break
A specialized neighborhood known for its unique architectural style
n: Answer: B — Lynch defines an 'edge' as a linear boundary that acts as a barrier or break between districts. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q166)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does Kevin Lynch define a 'district' in urban mapping terms?
o: A single prominent statue located at a major road intersection
A sharp boundary fence separating two private properties
A linear boundary that acts as a barrier or structural break
A medium-to-large section of a city that has a distinct, shared visual character that a person can mentally enter "inside" of
n: Answer: B — Lynch's 'district' is a medium-to-large area with a distinct, shared identity a person can mentally enter. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q167)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Jane Jacobs introduced 'eyes on the street.' What does that mean for neighborhood safety?
o: Buildings should have windows and active storefronts facing the sidewalk so residents naturally watch over the street.
Streets should be kept empty of pedestrians at night.
Police stations should sit on every residential block.
Cities should install CCTV cameras on every power pole.
n: Answer: A — Jane Jacobs's 'eyes on the street' means active windows and storefronts facing the sidewalk let residents naturally watch over it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q168)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Daniel Burnham led the early-1900s 'City Beautiful' movement. What core philosophy guided his approach to disorderly urban centers?
o: Leaving the city layout completely organic without any central planning rules
Replacing all public parks with high-efficiency vehicle parking decks
Moving all commercial shops underground to keep streets quiet
Creating monumental civic centers, wide boulevards, and classical beauty to inspire civic pride and order
n: Answer: A — Burnham's City Beautiful movement pursued monumental civic centers, wide boulevards, and classical grandeur to inspire civic order and pride. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q169)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Carlos Moreno's '15-Minute City' concept, popularized in the 2020s, aims to reorganize daily urban life around what schedule?
o: Requiring citizens to spend 15 minutes a day planting trees in public parks.
Ensuring high-speed commuter trains arrive at platforms every 15 minutes.
Ensuring daily necessities are reachable within a 15-minute drive from home.
Ensuring daily necessities are reachable within a 15-minute walk or bike ride from home.
n: Answer: C — Moreno's 15-Minute City aims to put daily necessities within a 15-minute walk or bike ride of home. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q170)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Patrick Geddes coined 'survey before plan.' What does this rule require of an architect or planner?
o: Pouring concrete road foundations before assigning zone uses.
Thoroughly studying a site's geography, history, culture, and population before drawing new layout plans.
Calculating a project's total financial profit before purchasing the land.
Interviewing neighboring city mayors to align zoning tax laws.
n: Answer: A — Geddes's 'survey before plan' calls for thoroughly studying a site's geography, history, culture, and people before laying out any plan. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q171)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Ebenezer Howard's 'Three Magnets' diagram illustrated forces pulling people toward different environments. What was his ideal destination magnet?
o: The Country (offering natural beauty but absolute economic isolation and lack of infrastructure)
The Wilderness (completely devoid of any human infrastructure or roads)
The Town (characterized by high wages but severe pollution and overcrowding)
The Town-Country (combining the economic opportunities of the city with the fresh air and open spaces of nature)
n: Answer: B — Howard's ideal 'Town-Country' magnet combined the economic opportunity of the city with the open space and nature of the countryside. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q172)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Futuristic 'floating city' concepts, such as the UN-backed Oceanix project, are engineered specifically to protect coastal populations from which global threat?
o: Extreme volcanic ash fallout events
Rising sea levels and severe coastal storm flooding caused by climate change
High-velocity tornado wind damage
Severe underground tectonic earthquake shaking
n: Answer: D — Floating city concepts like Oceanix are designed to protect coastal populations from rising seas and climate-driven storm flooding. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q173)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Le Corbusier's master plan for Chandigarh, India, drew on an anatomical analogy. How did he map the city's functional sectors onto the human body?
o: The whole city was shaped like a giant skeletal arm crossing a river.
Highway systems were the 'stomach,' schools were the 'eyes.'
Industrial factories were the 'brain,' residential homes were the 'feet.'
The capitol building was the 'head,' the central green parks were the 'lungs,' and the commercial center was the 'heart.'
n: Answer: A — Le Corbusier mapped Chandigarh's capitol as the 'Head,' its green parks as the 'Lungs,' and its commercial center as the 'Heart.' (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q174)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does Kevin Lynch mean by 'urban legibility'?
o: How easily a city's parts can be recognized and organized by residents into a coherent mental map.
The font size used on public highway wayfinding signs.
How easily zoning laws can be read and understood by lawyers.
The number of historic books held in a central public library.
n: Answer: C — Urban legibility is how easily residents can recognize and organize a city's parts into a coherent mental map. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q175)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Constantinos Doxiadis identified five core elements of any human settlement. Which one names the physical structures, houses, and buildings that shelter people?
o: Networks
Nature
Shells
Society
n: Answer: A — Of Doxiadis's five ekistic elements, 'Shells' are the physical buildings and structures that house people. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q176)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Before Spanish colonization, what geographic layout was most common for native Filipino barangay settlements?
o: Concentric circular rings expanding outward from a central temple.
Massive, dense stone cities hidden deep in mountain valleys.
Linear footprints along coastlines and riverbanks for easy transit, fishing, and trade.
A rigid gridiron system centered around stone palaces.
n: Answer: C — Pre-colonial barangays typically formed linear settlements along coasts and rivers for transit, fishing, and trade. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q177)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What was the typical population size and social structure of a pre-colonial Philippine barangay?
o: A small, self-sufficient, kinship-based community of 30 to 100 families led by a local chief called a Datu
A massive empire containing millions of citizens ruled by a single remote emperor
A dense network of industrial factory workers living in stone barracks
A temporary camp of 5 to 10 nomadic hunters who moved every single day
n: Answer: D — A pre-colonial barangay was a small, kinship-based community of roughly 30–100 families led by a Datu. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q178)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What was the main objective of the Spanish colonial government's Reducción policy across the Philippines?
o: To reduce how much land a farming family could use.
To reduce the total population of native settlements through forced migration.
To systematically group scattered, independent native communities into centralized towns, easing religious conversion and tax collection.
To replace timber buildings with lightweight bamboo structures.
n: Answer: B — The Reducción policy resettled scattered native communities into centralized towns to ease religious conversion and tax collection. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q179)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In 1573, King Philip II issued planning directives dictating how new Spanish colonial towns across the Americas and the Philippines had to be laid out. What is this document called?
o: The Laws of the Indies
The Tordesillas Urban Accord
The Burnham Manifesto
The Gridiron Mandate
n: Answer: D — King Philip II's 1573 planning code for Spanish colonial towns is known as the Laws of the Indies. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q180)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In a standard Philippine colonial plaza complex, where were the grand houses of the wealthy elite (Principalia) legally required to be built?
o: Stacked vertically atop the church bell tower.
On floating river rafts behind the municipal courthouse.
Miles away in rural agricultural zones for privacy.
Directly facing or immediately adjacent to the central plaza marketplace.
n: Answer: A — Colonial plaza complexes required the Principalia's grand houses to face or sit adjacent to the central plaza. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q181)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the scientific definition of the field of 'Ekistics'?
o: The architectural styling of interior residential furniture layouts
The engineering study of deep underground concrete foundations
The historical analysis of ancient Roman masonry equations
The comprehensive, multidisciplinary study of human settlements, examining their growth, scales, and structural elements
n: Answer: A — Ekistics is the comprehensive, multidisciplinary study of human settlements and their scale, growth, and structure. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q182)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which prominent American architect and planner visited the Philippines in 1904 to design City Beautiful master plans for Manila and Baguio City?
o: Louis Sullivan
Robert Moses
Frank Lloyd Wright
Daniel Burnham
n: Answer: D — Daniel Burnham visited the Philippines in 1904 to prepare City Beautiful master plans for Manila and Baguio. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q183)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: During the Spanish colonial period, what function did the Parian in Manila serve?
o: The main cemetery located behind the grand cathedral
The private residential palace of the Spanish Governor-General
A highly regulated commercial neighborhood located outside the walls of Intramuros, designated specifically for Chinese merchants and artisans
A stone aqueduct system that carried fresh drinking water to the city center
n: Answer: A — The Parian was the regulated commercial district outside Intramuros's walls designated for Chinese merchants and artisans. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q184)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Quezon City's planning began in 1939 under the Commonwealth government to serve as the new capital. Which design movement inspired its wide avenues, massive civic circles, and generous parks?
o: New Urbanism, focused exclusively on narrow, low-density rural carriage lanes.
The City Beautiful movement, prioritizing monumental axes, grand circles, and sprawling green parkways.
Deconstructivism, favoring fragmented, chaotic grids and asymmetrical paths.
Brutalism, favoring raw, exposed concrete mega-blocks with no open space.
n: Answer: A — Quezon City's 1939 plan of wide avenues and civic circles was directly inspired by the City Beautiful movement. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q185)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Constantinos Doxiadis predicted every city on Earth would eventually merge into a single worldwide urban network. What did he call this global-city concept?
o: Ecumenopolis
Megalopolis
Necropolis
Metropolis
n: Answer: B — Doxiadis called his hypothetical future of one continuous, planet-spanning city 'Ecumenopolis.' (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q186)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which of Kevin Lynch's five elements forms the primary network of a city's mental map — the channels people regularly travel along?
o: Paths
Landmarks
Edges
Nodes
n: Answer: C — Lynch's 'paths' are the channels — streets, walkways — along which people habitually travel. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q187)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Tony Garnier's 1904 'Industrial City' (Cité Industrielle) concept introduced what major zoning milestone in planning history?
o: It required all residential structures be built with cast-iron framing.
It concentrated the entire population inside a single royal palace ground.
It was the first model to strictly separate work areas from living areas for public health.
It banned electricity use in public commercial zones.
n: Answer: A — Tony Garnier's Cité Industrielle (1904) was among the first plans to strictly zone work areas apart from living areas. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q188)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which modernist architect wrote 'A house is a machine for living in,' framing architecture as a highly functional, engineered tool?
o: Kenzo Tange
Walter Gropius
Tadao Ando
Le Corbusier
n: Answer: A — Le Corbusier wrote that 'a house is a machine for living in' in Vers une architecture. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q189)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: If a historic public building has grand columns, a triangular pediment over its entrance, and a symmetrical stone façade echoing ancient Greek and Roman temples, what style is it?
o: Gothic Revival
Rococo
Neoclassical
Bauhaus
n: Answer: C — Grand columns, a pediment, and symmetrical stone facades echoing Greek/Roman temples define the Neoclassical style. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q190)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: When an architect designs benches, door handles, stair steps, and ceiling heights to match the comfortable reach and proportions of the human body, what principle is being applied?
o: Asymmetrical Contrast
Human Scale
Monumental Scale
Axial Symmetry
n: Answer: A — Designing fixtures and dimensions to match comfortable human reach and proportion is the principle of Human Scale. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q191)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What planning strategy shields quiet residential streets from fast-moving traffic by pushing high-speed roads to the perimeter of a large block?
o: Concentric Business Rings
Spot Zoning Plan
Ribbon Sprawl Layout
Superblock Design
n: Answer: D — Superblock design routes fast traffic around the perimeter of a large block, keeping the quiet residential interior free of through-traffic. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q192)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What was the core philosophy of the Postmodern architecture movement that emerged in the late 1960s and '70s?
o: Breaking strict modernist rules by reintroducing historical ornament, color, irony, and playful forms.
Banning all color and forcing buildings to resemble raw factory warehouses.
Moving all human residential space into deep underground cave networks.
Making every building perfectly round to mimic organic natural shapes.
n: Answer: C — Postmodernism reintroduced historical ornament, color, irony, and playful form in reaction against strict Modernist rules. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q193)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In master planning, what is the main benefit of designing a centralized park system or interconnected greenway network?
o: Increasing the density of high-rise commercial towers.
Maximizing space available for wide, multi-lane highways.
Acting as the city's 'green lungs' — cleaning air, managing stormwater, and offering public recreation space.
Concentrating all industrial factories into a single zone.
n: Answer: C — A connected park/greenway system serves as a city's 'green lungs,' managing stormwater, air quality, and recreation. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q194)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which 1920s-'30s design style features geometric patterns, bold sunburst motifs, chevron lines, and sleek metallic outlines, as seen atop the Chrysler Building?
o: Baroque
Neoclassical
Art Deco
Art Nouveau
n: Answer: D — Geometric sunbursts, chevrons, and sleek metallic lines atop buildings like the Chrysler Building define Art Deco. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q195)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which proportioning system uses a ratio found throughout nature (roughly 1 to 1.618) to build visually pleasing relationships between a building's width and height?
o: The Ken Dimension
The Modular Grid
The Ergonomic Metric
The Golden Section
n: Answer: A — The Golden Section is the roughly 1:1.618 ratio found throughout nature and applied to pleasing architectural proportions. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q196)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In neighborhood planning, what is the main traffic-safety benefit of a cul-de-sac (a dead-end street with a circular turnaround)?
o: Increasing the speed of cross-town vehicle commutes.
Cutting the cost of installing public sewers.
Keeping fast, through-traffic from cutting through quiet residential blocks.
Maximizing commercial retail space along the road.
n: Answer: B — A cul-de-sac's dead-end turnaround keeps fast through-traffic from cutting through quiet residential streets. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q197)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which urban road layout combines a traditional rectangular grid with diagonal avenues meeting at central public squares or monumental civic circles?
o: Multi-Nuclei Mesh
Concentric Ring Plan
Radial-Gridiron Plan
Linear Network
n: Answer: C — A Radial-Gridiron plan overlays diagonal boulevards onto a rectangular grid, meeting at civic circles or squares. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q198)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Known as the 'Queen of the Curve,' which architect designed futuristic, fluid buildings like the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku using advanced digital modeling?
o: Maya Lin
Neri Oxman
Zaha Hadid
Kazuyo Sejima
n: Answer: C — Zaha Hadid, nicknamed the 'Queen of the Curve,' designed the fluid, digitally modeled Heydar Aliyev Center. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q199)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In a traditional Bahay na Bato, what is the 'Volada'?
o: A secret underground drainage tunnel used to flush out water during torrential rainstorms
The decorative iron grillwork installed on windows to protect the family from intruders
An overhanging, enclosed wooden gallery or corridor on the second floor that shades the lower floor and allows air to circulate around the house
A solid stone foundation wall that completely seals off the ground floor storage area
n: Answer: C — The volada is an overhanging, enclosed second-floor wooden gallery that shades the ground floor and allows air to circulate. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q200)
